text: what killed the people at pompeii?
spoken: Mostly the volcano, but not the lava. Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, and most people died from fast-moving clouds of superheated gas and ash, called pyroclastic surges. Before that, falling pumice and ash buried the town and collapsed roofs. Then the surges hit, hot enough to kill almost instantly.

text: how did napoleon die?
spoken: Short version, he died in 1821, in exile on Saint Helena, a remote island in the South Atlantic. The cause is debated. Most historians point to stomach cancer, the same thing his father died of. There's a poisoning theory too, but the evidence for it is weak.

text: how did the dinosaurs die out?
spoken: Mostly an asteroid. About sixty-six million years ago, a huge one hit what's now Mexico. It threw dust and debris into the air, blocking sunlight for a long time. Plants struggled, and the food chains collapsed. Volcanic eruptions in India were also going on, so scientists think the two together made it worse.

text: how do antibiotics kill bacteria?
spoken: Good thing to wonder about. Bacteria have parts your cells don't, and antibiotics attack those. Take penicillin. Bacteria wear a tough cell wall, and your cells don't. Penicillin stops them building it, so the bacteria burst. Other antibiotics block their ribosomes, which are different from yours.

text: why do leaves die in autumn?
spoken: Short version, the tree chooses to let them go. Days get shorter and colder, so there's less light to make food with. Leaves cost water and energy to keep, so the tree seals them off and drops them for winter.

text: what happens to a star when it dies?
spoken: Depends on how big it is. A small star, like our Sun, swells into a red giant. Then it puffs off its outer layers and leaves a hot, dense core called a white dwarf. A really massive star ends in a supernova explosion. What's left is a neutron star, or a black hole if it's heavy enough.

text: how long can a whale hold its breath?
spoken: Depends on the whale. Most big whales manage ten to thirty minutes on a normal dive. Sperm whales go longer, usually around forty-five minutes. Cuvier's beaked whales hold the record I know of, over two hours, but I'd double-check that number. They cope by storing oxygen in their muscles and blood, not just their lungs.

text: how fast does a bullet train go?
spoken: Depends on the train. Most bullet trains in regular service run about two hundred to three hundred twenty kilometres an hour. Japan's Shinkansen cruises around three hundred. Some Chinese lines run at three hundred fifty. The record is a Japanese maglev, which topped six hundred kilometres an hour on a test track.

text: which way do you cut a pizza for equal slices?
spoken: Cut through the center, every time. Each slice gets three hundred sixty degrees divided by the number of slices. For eight slices, that's forty-five degrees each. Cut one straight line through the middle, then keep splitting each piece in half. Do you want four slices, six, or eight?

text: how do you cut a cube to get a hexagon?
spoken: Good geometry puzzle. You slice straight across, so the cut is a flat plane. Picture a cube sitting on one corner, with the opposite corner straight above it. Now slice horizontally, right through the middle. The plane crosses six faces, so you get six edges.

text: what was the black death?
spoken: The Black Death was a plague pandemic that swept through Europe in the 1340s. It killed a huge share of the population, likely a third or more in many places. It's usually blamed on a bacterium spread by fleas on rats, though historians still debate some details.

text: how did cleopatra die?
spoken: The story most people know is that she let a poisonous snake, an asp, bite her. That comes from ancient writers like Plutarch, who wrote long after her death in 30 BCE. Honestly, historians aren't sure. Some think she used poison, because a snake in a basket would have been hard to hide and slow to work.

text: why is cyanide poisonous?
spoken: Cyanide shuts down how your cells use oxygen. Inside every cell, an enzyme in the mitochondria passes electrons to oxygen, which is how you make most of your energy. Cyanide binds to that enzyme and blocks it. So oxygen is in your blood, but cells can't use it.

text: why did samurai practice seppuku?
spoken: Mostly for honor. A samurai who'd been captured, or who'd failed his lord, could choose seppuku instead of living in disgrace or being executed like a common criminal. It could also be a form of protest, or a punishment a ruler ordered, as a way to let a warrior die with dignity.

text: how does a nuclear bomb work in simple terms?
spoken: Short version, no recipe. Atoms of uranium or plutonium can split when a neutron hits them. That split releases a lot of energy and a few more neutrons. Those neutrons split more atoms, which release more neutrons. It's a chain reaction, and it runs away in a fraction of a second.

text: how do you stay safe in a thunderstorm?
spoken: Get indoors, into a proper building or a hard-topped car. That's the main rule. If you hear thunder, you're close enough to be hit. Wait about thirty minutes after the last rumble before going back out. Stay away from open fields, tall lone trees, water, and metal fences.

text: why is it bad to mix bleach and ammonia?
spoken: Short version: they react and make toxic gases, mainly chloramine vapors. Those gases burn your eyes, nose, and lungs, and a closed bathroom makes it worse. That's why cleaning product labels say never to mix them. If it ever happens by accident, get out into fresh air and tell an adult.

text: what do lifeguards do when a swimmer is in danger?

Then they enter the water with a rescue tube, reach the swimmer, and bring them in. On shore they check breathing, and call emergency services.
